query: Which material can be used for enhance glass-forming ability, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Introducing high chemical complexity by designing a multi‐principal element alloy—in particular, using the CrMnFeCoNi system—enhances glass‐forming ability. This is because the high mixing entropy and the atomic size mismatch inherent to such high‐entropy alloys frustrate crystallization during rapid cooling.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional crystalline single‐phase CrMnFeCoNi high‐entropy alloy produced by casting or other standard methods
generation.intervention: Apply rapid solidification (e.g., using high cooling rates or additive manufacturing techniques with controlled quenching) to promote amorphization
generation.conditions: Processing under high cooling rates such that the alloy is cooled through the crystallization temperature window faster than atomic rearrangements can occur, while keeping the overall composition at near equiatomic proportions
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced atomic-level disorder arising from increased mixing entropy and atomic size mismatches in the alloy
generation.mechanism: The ‘cocktail effect’ in multi‐principal element systems increases the nucleation barrier for crystals; combined with fast cooling, this effect hinders the diffusion and ordering of atoms, thereby promoting the formation of an amorphous (glass) phase
generation.predicted_outcome: A reduction in the critical cooling rate needed to form a glassy state and an enlarged glass-forming region in the alloy’s phase diagram compared to conventional alloys
generation.baseline: Conventional binary or ternary alloys that lack the enhanced chemical complexity and suffer from easier nucleation of crystalline phases
generation.boundary: The improvement in glass-forming ability is anticipated only under processing conditions that enforce rapid cooling. Under slow cooling or in alloys with lower mixing entropy, crystallization will dominate
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvement in glass-forming ability (e.g., the reduction in the critical cooling rate) and the optimal compositional window for the CrMnFeCoNi system remain uncertain until experimentally verified

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples: one set consisting of the conventional crystalline CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy and another with a deliberately optimized high mixing entropy composition. Subject both sets to identical rapid solidification processes (e.g., via splat quenching or controlled additive manufacturing under high cooling rates). Analyze the resulting microstructures using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to determine the extent of amorphization.
measurements: Critical cooling rate required for glass formation (determined via DSC)
Volume fraction of amorphous phase (evaluated by XRD and microscopy)
Thermal stability of the amorphous phase
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high mixing entropy alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant lower critical cooling rate or a higher amorphous phase fraction compared to the conventional alloy (under identical processing and environmental conditions), the hypothesis that increased chemical complexity enhances glass-forming ability will be falsified.

4.1. Phase Formation

Although a lack of HEA phase diagrams limit the availability of thermodynamic data, some thermodynamic properties, such as atomic size, melting point, mixing entropy, mixing enthalpy, and valence electron concentration, can be used as criteria to predict the phase formation in the HEA system. According to the empirical rules, BCC solid solutions were generally formed in HEA systems under the following certain conditions. (1) The electron concentration (VEC) was lower than 6.87 [ [26] ]; (2) a new parameter combining effects of entropy and enthalpy (Ω) was proposed to be more than 1 and atomic size differences (δ) was less than 6.6% [ [27] ]. δ, Ω, and VEC are calculated to be 5.4, 2.92 and 4.80 respectively, so BCC solid solution could be anticipated, which tallied well with the research results produced by H. Chen et al. [ [13] ]. Guo et al. [ [28] ] further proposed that all ductile alloys have a VEC ≤ 4.4, while all brittle alloys have a VEC ≥ 4.6. Therefore, the NbMoCrTiAl RHEA should be without ductility and it is indeed a type of brittle RHEA.
